snip.t: Guillain‑Barre syndrome (GBS) – an acute, immune‑mediated polyradiculoneuropathy characterised by rapidly progressive, symmetric weakness with areflexia, often preceded by an infection.

| Guillain‑Barre syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) | Acute onset ≤4 weeks, rapid ascending weakness, areflexia, preceding infection, autonomic signs | CSF albumin‑cytologic dissociation, nerve‑conduction slowing, need for ventilatory monitoring |

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a child with suspected GBS? — CSF analysis for albuminocytologic dissociation.
A child with ascending weakness and areflexia is deteriorating rapidly. What is the next step? — Assess respiratory function and consider intubation.
Which treatment is preferred if IVIg is unavailable? — Plasma exchange.
How would you differentiate GBS from myasthenia gravis at the bedside? — Look for fatigable weakness and response to edrophonium.
What autonomic sign would prompt urgent transfer to ICU? — Severe hypertension or tachycardia with labile BP.
Why is early physiotherapy important in GBS? — It prevents contractures and aids recovery.
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: An acute, immune‑mediated polyradiculoneuropathy presenting with rapidly progressive, symmetric weakness and areflexia, often after an infection. Early recognition and supportive care are vital.

sections.p: Guillain‑Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune‑mediated polyradiculoneuropathy. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) albuminocytologic dissociation and nerve conduction studies.

t.b: Does the patient have albuminocytologic dissociation? — Elevated protein > 45 mg/dL with normal cell count indicates GBS.
Is there demyelination or axonal loss? — Slowed conduction velocity or conduction block supports GBS.
Are deep tendon reflexes absent? — Areflexia is a key clinical sign.

b: 1 – Mild weakness, able to walk 10 m
2 – Moderate weakness, needs assistance to walk
3 – Severe weakness, cannot walk, needs assistance
4 – Respiratory failure or severe autonomic dysfunction
sections.p: The Hughes Functional Grading Scale (0–6) is used to stage severity and guide monitoring.
GBS is triggered by an aberrant immune response to a preceding infection. In low‑resource settings, common antecedents include diarrhoeal illness, upper respiratory tract infection, and malaria.
Patients present with a sudden, progressive, symmetric limb weakness that ascends from the feet. Reflexes are lost, and autonomic dysfunction may appear.
Investigations confirm the diagnosis and rule out mimics. In settings where advanced tests are unavailable, focus on clinical criteria and basic labs.

t.b: Is protein elevated with normal cell count? — Supports GBS.
Are potassium or calcium abnormal? — Electrolyte disturbances can mimic weakness.
Is there anemia or infection? — Helps exclude other causes.
Is there diaphragmatic elevation? — Indicates respiratory compromise.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include rapid progression to respiratory failure, severe autonomic instability, and cranial nerve involvement.

b: IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or plasma exchange
sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying immune attack, preventing complications, and providing supportive care.

t.b: Does the patient receive IVIg? — Provides passive antibodies to halt immune attack.
Is plasma exchange feasible? — Removes circulating autoantibodies when IVIg unavailable.
Is the patient breathing adequately? — Intubation required if PaO2 <60 mmHg or SpO2 <90%.

sections.p: Follow‑up focuses on rehabilitation and monitoring for relapse. Prevention centers on early treatment of infections and vaccination where applicable.

b: Myasthenia gravis – fatigable weakness, positive edrophonium test
Tick paralysis – sudden onset, reversible after tick removal
sections.p: Conditions that mimic GBS include myasthenia gravis, botulism, tick paralysis, and metabolic myopathies.

b: Early CSF protein <45 mg/dL – repeat after 1 week
sections.p: CSF protein may be normal early; nerve conduction studies can be normal in axonal variants; normal electrolytes do not exclude metabolic myopathies.
